Series::pile¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::pile(pluss::RangeView<Series> others,
             std::int64_t dim = 0) const -> Series

What It Does¶

Stacks self with one or more peer series along a new axis.

Conceptually, pile() is stack: unlike unite(), it does not extend an existing axis. Instead, it inserts a new axis of length equal to the number of inputs (1 + others.size()) and places each input in one slice along that axis.

self always occupies slice 0 on the new axis, then others fill slices 1, 2, and so on.

Parameters¶

others (pluss::RangeView<Series>)

The additional series to stack after self.

All inputs must:

  • live on the same platform

  • have exactly the same shape

  • have exactly the same dtype

Unlike unite(), there is no dtype-promotion toggle here. Stacking is strict.

dim (std::int64_t)

Where the new axis should be inserted. Negative indexing is supported against the output rank (self.dim() + 1).

For a 2 x 2 input:

  • dim = 0 yields [n, 2, 2]

  • dim = 1 yields [2, n, 2]

  • dim = -1 yields [2, 2, n]

Returns¶

Series A new series with one extra axis containing the stacked inputs.

Gradient¶

pile() is differentiable in every tracked input. Backward selects the slice of the outgoing sensitivity corresponding to each input’s position on the new axis and routes that slice back to the input.

This is the exact structural mirror of the forward op:

  • input 0 receives out_sens.select(dim, 0)

  • input 1 receives out_sens.select(dim, 1)

  • and so on

Examples¶

Example 1. Stack two 2 x 2 inputs along a new leading axis.

auto left = pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3, 4}, {2, 2});
auto right = pluss::make_series({10, 20, 30, 40}, {2, 2});
std::cout << left.pile({right}, 0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2,2], strides=[4,2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=8, contiguous=true)
data=[[[1, 2],
  [3, 4]],
  [[10, 20],
  [30, 40]]]

The new axis has length 2: slice 0 is left, slice 1 is right.

Example 2. A trailing new axis gives a different layout story even though the same two inputs participate.

std::cout << left.pile({right}, -1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2,2], strides=[4,2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=8, contiguous=true)
data=[[[1, 10],
  [2, 20]],
  [[3, 30],
  [4, 40]]]

Now the new axis is the last one, so each original scalar position has become the pair [left_value, right_value].

Example 3. Shape mismatch is rejected.

try {
  auto bad_shape = pluss::make_series({5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10}, {3, 2});
  std::cout << left.pile({bad_shape}, 0);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

stack: shape mismatch

This method is intentionally stricter than unite(): because it is creating a new axis rather than extending one, every preexisting axis must already agree exactly.

Example 4. Backward selects each input’s slice along the new axis.

auto tracked_left = pluss::make_series(
    {1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0}, {2, 2});
auto tracked_right = pluss::make_series(
    {10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0}, {2, 2});
tracked_left.tracks_slope_(true);
tracked_right.tracks_slope_(true);

auto stacked = tracked_left.pile({tracked_right}, 1);
stacked.sum().reverse();
std::cout << "dleft=" << tracked_left.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "dright=" << tracked_right.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

dleft=pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=false)
data=[[1, 1],
  [1, 1]]
dright=pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=false)
data=[[1, 1],
  [1, 1]]

The sensitivities are all ones because stacked.sum() touched every output position once. The key point is structural: each parent receives the slice of the stacked output that it originally occupied.

Notes¶

  • pile() inserts a new axis; unite() does not.

  • All input shapes must match exactly.

  • The result is materialized, not aliased.

See Also¶

  • Series::unite: concatenate along an existing axis instead.

  • Series::unsqueeze: the conceptual one-input version of creating a new axis before alignment.
